synthetic_samples.reference_summary: The first fan bank's start threshold in the temperature controller was retained at 92°C rather than 78°C. The cooling control logic used an ambient bias that remained at zero when the outdoor temperature exceeded 43°C. Although ambient temperature was 47°C, this value alone was not the root cause; the transformer load was only 75 percent of rating. A 40 MVA auxiliary transformer was taken out of service, raising the station load demand on the target transformer. The manual selector blocked this remote command; the pump did not energise. The leaked current shifted the reported top-oil temperature downward by 6°C continuously. At 15:04, the winding hot-spot relay operated and sent a trip signal to the transformer circuit breaker. The Synthetic Grid network lost 116 MW of firm supply when the 220 kV ring separated. After the trip, two technicians manually closed the cooling valve and turned both pump switches to forced-run. The control algorithms were replaced with the archived 2019 revision, resetting the start setpoint to 78°C.

semantic_core.text: The first fan bank's start threshold in the temperature controller was retained at 92°C rather than 78°C.
The cooling control logic used an ambient bias that remained at zero when the outdoor temperature exceeded 43°C.
The hand-off-auto selector for the entire cooler group sat in manual without its lockwire.
A 6 A ground-fault current leaked into the analogue temperature input through old cable insulation; the leak was present for months before the trip.
Although ambient temperature was 47°C, this value alone was not the root cause; the transformer load was only 75 percent of rating.
A 40 MVA auxiliary transformer was taken out of service, raising the station load demand on the target transformer.
The step-down transformer's oil temperature increased from 88°C to 105°C during a 20-minute interval.
The supervisor dispatched a remote start command to the oil pump at 14:56.
The manual selector blocked this remote command; the pump did not energise.
The leaked current shifted the reported top-oil temperature downward by 6°C continuously.
The SCADA trend recorded 99°C, while a calibrated gauge at the transformer showed 105°C.
Confident in the lower reading, the shift charge engineer reduced the alarm threshold to 103°C.
At 15:04, the winding hot-spot relay operated and sent a trip signal to the transformer circuit breaker.
The Synthetic Grid network lost 116 MW of firm supply when the 220 kV ring separated.
Fourteen customers under the feeder experienced voltage dips between 31% and 45% for about 700 ms.
The post-event oil sample displayed ethylene above 1100 ppm, indicating severe thermal stress.
After the trip, two technicians manually closed the cooling valve and turned both pump switches to forced-run.
The control algorithms were replaced with the archived 2019 revision, resetting the start setpoint to 78°C.
Engineers repaired the cable insulation and recalibrated the analogue input card using a precision source.
The transformer remained at 70% MVA load for 24 hours until all thermal indications returned to normal.

synthetic_samples.reference_summary: The cooling controller's integrator error was negative; valve reference fell while temperature rose. The outdoor air sensor was mounted in a still pocket, far from the natural draft. The day was hot, yet the 48.5°C peak was not the primary cause of the shutdown; load had been within 98% of planned limits. A 55 kVA motor-driven pump started, reducing the oil level in the sump and triggering the low-level switch. The inlet valve remained at its minimum stop, overruled by the negative integrator. The fan speed reduction forced the top-oil temperature to increase at a rate of 1.4 K per minute. The transformer relay detached the incoming feeder at 17:13 and isolated the faulty bay. The synthetic local load received a 35% voltage drop for 1.8 seconds before the capacitor banks switched out. The operator manually opened the inlet valve using a 500 mm wrench after local confirmation. Portable fans were directed at the radiator intake until the oil trend reached 70°C.

semantic_core.text: The cooling controller's integrator error was negative; valve reference fell while temperature rose.
The outdoor air sensor was mounted in a still pocket, far from the natural draft.
A 20 mm layer of dust insulated the cooling thermostat bubble from the pipe.
The dc battery voltage collapsed to 68 V for several seconds under unbalanced charging.
The day was hot, yet the 48.5°C peak was not the primary cause of the shutdown; load had been within 98% of planned limits.
A 55 kVA motor-driven pump started, reducing the oil level in the sump and triggering the low-level switch.
The control loop setpoint switched to cold reserve via an unbalanced automation state.
At 17:11, the transformer protection saw a maximum winding temperature of 172°C.
The inlet valve remained at its minimum stop, overruled by the negative integrator.
The fan speed reduction forced the top-oil temperature to increase at a rate of 1.4 K per minute.
Operators relied on the instantaneous analogue indication, ignoring the stale trend for 15 minutes.
The hot oil release continued past the rupture, and the safety valve began to chatter.
The transformer relay detached the incoming feeder at 17:13 and isolated the faulty bay.
The synthetic local load received a 35% voltage drop for 1.8 seconds before the capacitor banks switched out.
Factory output at Synthetic Park stopped for 38 minutes after the low-voltage tripping.
An oil leak of 25 litres formed, contaminating the concrete bund and raising environmental concern.
The operator manually opened the inlet valve using a 500 mm wrench after local confirmation.
Portable fans were directed at the radiator intake until the oil trend reached 70°C.
Control engineers ramped the integrator gain down to 0.1 and re-initialised the setpoint block.
The transformer re-entered service after a six-hour stabilisation at 40 percent capacity.
